units.title: Money and Financial Institutions
units.intro:
Barter needs a double coincidence of wants. Money kills that problem. Functions: medium of exchange, unit of account, store of value (and sometimes standard of deferred payment). Good money is durable, portable, divisible, scarce, acceptable.

Banks take deposits, keep a fraction as reserve, lend the rest — that is how credit multiplies (school picture). Central bank (or the state’s bank) issues notes, holds reserves, tries to keep the currency trusted. Other institutions: insurance, microfinance, savings groups — the book’s local list.

cards.title: 2.1 Money
body: During primitive modes of production, each community produces for its own needs.
For example, farmers concentrate on farming, herders concentrate on cattle raising, shoe makers concentrate on making shoes, etc.
Before the introduction of money, there was a system of trading known as barter.
Exchange is the process of obtaining desirable objects by offering something else in return.
The existence of the primitive barter economy shows that exchange was possible without money.

cards.title: MUSE
body: Medium, Unit of account, Store of value, (deferred) Exchange settlement. Inflation steals the store-of-value job — too much money chasing goods.

cards.title: More depth
body: Commodity money (gold, salt, cattle) vs token / fiat (the note is money because the law and trust say so). Cheques and electronic transfers are claims on bank money. Liquidity = how fast an asset becomes spending power without losing value. Cash is most liquid; a building is not.

cards.title: Step-by-step
cards.problem: Which of the following is considered the most serious limitation of the barter system of exchange?

steps.text: **Step 1: Analyze the barter economy constraints**
In a barter economy, trade requires that two individuals each possess a good that the other desires.
**Step 2: Define double coincidence of wants**
This requirement is known as the **double coincidence of wants**.
Because finding such matching desires is highly unlikely and time-consuming, it is the most significant transaction barrier of barter.

cards.answer: The lack of a double coincidence of wants

steps.text: **Step 1: Define paper money categories**

**Step 2: Match with the question description**

cards.title: 2.2 Banks and Banking Activities
body: The financial system moves the economy’s scarce resources from savers (people who spend less than they earn) to borrowers (people who spend more than they earn).
Savers save for various reasons—to meet unforeseen emergencies or to live comfortably during retirement age.
Savers supply their money to the financial system and they will get back the principal with interest at a later date.
Borrowers demand money from the financial system and they will be required to pay back the principal and interest at a later date.
The financial system is made up of various financial institutions.

body: Interest = price of borrowed money
Simple I = Prt (Grade 11 maths also). Savers receive interest; borrowers pay it.

cards.title: 2.3 Insurance
body: Individuals face different types of losses or damages for different reasons.
Others will experience destruction of their homes and personal property because of fire, floods, earthquake or other disasters.
Still others will become disabled because of heart disease, cancer, AIDS, or other diseases.
Risk is defined as uncertainty concerning the occurrence of a loss.
For example, the risk of being killed in an accident is present because uncertainty is present.

cards.q: A bank account that allows the depositor to write cheques to make payments and withdraw funds at any time without restriction, but typically pays zero interest, is known as a:
cards.why:
**Step 1: Distinguish between deposit accounts**
- Savings Account: Earns interest, has withdrawal limits, no cheque facility.
- Current Account (or Chequing Account): Allows unlimited transactions, writing cheques, but pays no interest.

**Step 2: Match with description**
The question describes a chequing-enabled, zero-interest account, which is a **Current account**.

glossary.meaning: Barter is the exchange of goods for goods without the use of money.
Money is a stock of quantities measured at a particular point in time.
Inflation occurs when there is a general rise in prices without a corresponding increase in productivity.
Deflation is a decline in general price levels, often caused by a reduction in the supply of money or credit.
A central bank is the only authorized bank by law to print money.
Store of value In any society, there is a need to hold wealth in some form or another.
Risk is defined as uncertainty concerning the occurrence of a loss.
Insurance is defined as a form of cooperation through which all those who are open to risks and losses pool their resources and compensate those who suffer a loss.
Therefore, paper money is a legal tender because the law obliges everybody in society to accept it in payment of goods and services as well as in payment of debts.
Exchange is the process of obtaining desirable objects by offering something else in return.
Income is a flow variable measured over a period of time.
Liquidity is the relative ease and speed with which an asset can be converted into cash.
Financial markets are the institutions through which a person who wants to save can directly supply funds to a person who wants to borrow.
Banks are the financial intermediaries with which people are most familiar.
Deposits are the amount of money put in a bank by a customer.
Pooling is the spreading of losses incurred by the few over the entire group, so that in the process, average loss is substituted for actual loss.

tips.text: Before the introduction of money, there was a system of exchange called barter.
Barter is defined as the exchange of goods for goods without the use of money.
The functioning of a barer economy was, however, difficult and inconvenient.

The problems of the barter exchange include the absence of double coincidence of wants, lack of standard measurement during transaction, lack of divisibility, difficulty of storage, etc. These problems made barter a cumbersome and inefficient means of exchange.
The problems encountered and the inefficiency observed in a barter economy led to the invention of money.
Money is defined as anything that is generally accepted in payment for goods and services or in payment of debts.
The introduction of money in an economy solved the problems of barter and facilitated the exchange of goods and services and made efficiency and specialization possible.
Money has four basic functions in an economy: (i) as a medium of exchange, (ii) as a unit of account, (iii) as a store of value, and (iv) as a standard of deferred payments.
Different forms of money have been used in different periods of time in different societies.
Commodity money was the first form to be used to facilitate transaction.
Formula: Interest = price of borrowed money Simple I = Prt (Grade 11 maths also). Savers receive interest; borrowers pay it.
